### Africa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Africa")]

The most widespread of the native African games is [Mancala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancala "Mancala"). Mancala is a family of board games played around the world, sometimes called "[sowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sowing "Sowing")" games, or "count-and-capture" games, which describes the gameplay. The word _mancala:منقلة_ comes from the [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language") word _naqala:نقلة_ meaning literally "to move". The earliest evidence of [Mancala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mancala "Mancala") consists of fragments of pottery boards and several rock cuts found in [Aksumite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum "Kingdom of Aksum") in Ethiopia, [Matara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matara,_Eritrea "Matara, Eritrea") (now in [Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea")), and [Yeha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeha "Yeha") (also in Ethiopia), which have been dated by archaeologists to between the 6th and 7th century CE. More than 800 names of traditional mancala games are known, and almost 200 invented games have been described. However, some names denote the same game, while some names are used for more than one game. Today, the game is played worldwide, with [many distinct variants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mancala_games "List of mancala games") representing different regions of the world. Some historians believe that mancala is the oldest game in the world based on the archaeological evidence found in [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan") that dates around 6000 BC. The game might have been played by ancient [Nabataeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabataeans "Nabataeans") and could have been an ancient version of the modern mancala game.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-54)

### Americas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Americas")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Macuilxochitl_Patolli.png/250px-Macuilxochitl_Patolli.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Macuilxochitl_Patolli.png)

Patolli game being watched by [Macuilxochitl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xochipilli "Xochipilli") as depicted on page 048 of the [Codex Magliabechiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Magliabechiano "Codex Magliabechiano")

Archaeologist Barbara Voorhies has theorized that a series of holes on clay floors arranged in c shapes at the Tlacuachero archaeological site in Mexico's Chiapas state may be 5000-year-old dice-game scoreboards. If so this would be the oldest archaeological evidence for a game in the Americas.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-55)

[Dice games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dice_games "Dice games") were popular throughout the Americas. [Patolli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patolli "Patolli") was one of the most popular board games played by [Mesoamerican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican "Mesoamerican") peoples such as the [Mayans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_peoples "Maya peoples"), [Toltecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toltecs "Toltecs") and [Aztecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztecs "Aztecs"), it was a [race game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_game "Race game") played with beans or dice on square and oval-shaped boards and gambling was a key aspect of it. The Andean peoples also played a dice game which is called by the [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_languages "Quechua languages") word _pichca_ or _pisca_.

One of the oldest known ball games in history is the [Mesoamerican ballgame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_ballgame "Mesoamerican ballgame") (_Ōllamaliztli_ in [Nahuatl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahuatl "Nahuatl")). _Ōllamaliztli_ was played as far back as 1,400 BC and had important religious significance for the [mesoamerican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican "Mesoamerican") peoples such as the [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization "Maya civilization") and [Aztec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec "Aztec").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-FOX-56) The game evolved over time, but the main goal was to keep a solid rubber ball in play by striking it with various parts of the body or with tools such as rackets. The game may have served as a proxy for warfare and also had a major religious function. Formal ballgames were held as ritual events, often featuring [human sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_sacrifice "Human sacrifice"), though it was also played for leisure by children and even women.

The [indigenous North American peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") played various kinds of [stickball games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_North_American_stickball "Indigenous North American stickball"), which are the ancestors of modern [lacrosse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrosse "Lacrosse"). Traditional stickball games were sometimes major events that could last several days. As many as 100 to 1,000 men from opposing villages or tribes would participate. The games were played in open plains located between villages, and the goals could range from 500 yards (460 m) to 6 miles (9.7 km) apart.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-STX-57)

### Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Europe")]

The [Tafl games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tafl_games "Tafl games") were a family of ancient [Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_tribes "Germanic tribes") and [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") board games played across much of Northern Europe from earlier than 400 CE until the 12th century.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-58) Although the rules of the games were never explicitly recorded, it seems to have been a game with uneven forces (2:1 ratio) and the goal of one side was to escape to the side of the board with a King while the other side's goal was to capture him. Tafl was spread by the [Vikings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vikings "Vikings") throughout northern Europe, including [Iceland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland"), [Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain "Great Britain"), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland"), and [Sápmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A1pmi "Sápmi").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-59)

Chess was introduced to the Iberian [emirate of Cordoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Cordoba "Emirate of Cordoba") in 822 during the reign of [Abd ar-Rahman II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_ar-Rahman_II "Abd ar-Rahman II"). By the middle of the 10th century, it was being played in Christian Spain, Italy and Southern Germany. By 1200, it had reached Britain and Scandinavia.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-60) Initially there were many differing local Chess games with varying rules or _assizes_ such as [Short assize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_assize "Short assize") chess, [Courier chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courier_chess "Courier chess") and [Dice Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dice_Chess "Dice Chess").

An important source of medieval games is the _[Libro de los juegos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libro\_de\_los\_juegos "Libro de los juegos")_, ("Book of games"), or _Libro de acedrex, dados e tablas_, ("Book of chess, dice and tables", in Old Spanish) which was commissioned by [Alfonso X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_X "Alfonso X") of Castile, Galicia and León in 1283.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-SMG-61) The manuscript contains descriptions and color illustrations of [dice games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dice_games "Dice games"), [chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") and [tabula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabula_(game) "Tabula (game)"), a predecessor of [backgammon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backgammon "Backgammon"). The book portrays these games within an astrological context, and some game variants are astronomically designed, such as a game titled "[astronomical chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_chess "Astronomical chess")", played on a board of seven concentric circles, divided radially into twelve areas, each associated with a constellation of the [Zodiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zodiac "Zodiac"). The symbolism of the text indicates that some of these games were given metaphysical significance. Chess was also used to teach social and moral lessons by the Dominican friar [Jacobus de Cessolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobus_de_Cessolis "Jacobus de Cessolis") in his _Liber de moribus hominum et officiis nobilium super ludo scacchorum_ ('Book of the customs of men and the duties of nobles or the Book of Chess'). Published circa 1300, the book was immensely popular.

Other pre-modern European board games include [Rithmomachy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rithmomachy "Rithmomachy") or "the philosophers game", [alquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alquerque "Alquerque"), [fox & geese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_&_geese "Fox & geese"), [nine men's morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_men's_morris "Nine men's morris"), [draughts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draughts "Draughts"), [nim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nim "Nim"), [catch the hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_the_hare "Catch the hare") and the [game of the goose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_the_goose "Game of the goose"). [Dice games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dice_games "Dice games") were widely played throughout Europe and included [hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_(game) "Hazard (game)"), [chuck-a-luck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck-a-luck "Chuck-a-luck"), [Glückshaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gl%C3%BCckshaus "Glückshaus"), [shut the box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shut_the_box "Shut the box") and [knucklebones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knucklebones "Knucklebones").

[Card games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_games "Card games") first arrived in Italy from [Mamluk Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate_(Cairo) "Mamluk Sultanate (Cairo)") in the 14th century, with suits very similar to the Swords, Clubs, Cups and Coins and those still used in traditional [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_playing_cards "Italian playing cards") and [Spanish decks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_playing_cards "Spanish playing cards").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-62) The four [suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suit_(cards) "Suit (cards)") most commonly encountered today (spades, hearts, diamonds, and clubs) appear to have originated in France circa 1480.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-63) 1440s Italy saw the rise of [tarot cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarot_cards "Tarot cards") and this led to the development of [tarot card games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarot_card_games "Tarot card games") such as [tarocchini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarocchini "Tarocchini"), [Königrufen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nigrufen "Königrufen") and [French tarot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_tarot "French tarot").

Outdoor games were very popular during holidays and fairs and were played by all classes. Many of these games are the predecessors of modern sports and [lawn games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_game "Lawn game"). [Boules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boules "Boules"), [lawn billiards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucco "Trucco") (later brought indoors as [billiards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billiards "Billiards")), [skittles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skittles_(sport) "Skittles (sport)") (an ancestor of modern ten pin [bowling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowling "Bowling")), [medieval football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_football "Medieval football"), [kolven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolven "Kolven"), [stoolball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoolball "Stoolball") (an ancestor of [cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket")), _[jeu de paume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeu\_de\_paume "Jeu de paume")_ (early racket-less [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis")), [horseshoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoes_(game) "Horseshoes (game)") and [quoits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quoits "Quoits") all predate the [early modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern "Early modern") era.

## Modern games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Modern games")]

### Professional board games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Professional board games")]

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Lasker-Steinitz.jpg/250px-Lasker-Steinitz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lasker-Steinitz.jpg)

[Emanuel Lasker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emanuel_Lasker "Emanuel Lasker") (right) playing Steinitz for the [World Chess Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Championship "World Chess Championship"), New York 1894

[Modern chess rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rules_of_chess "Rules of chess") began taking shape in Spain and Italy during the 15th century with the adoption of the standard Queen and Bishop movements (initially called "Mad Queen chess"). Writings on [chess theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_theory "Chess theory") also began to appear in the 15th century with the first text being the _Repetición de Amores y Arte de Ajedrez_ (Repetition of Love and the Art of Playing Chess, 1497) by Spanish churchman Luis Ramirez de Lucena. Chess books by authors such as [Ruy López de Segura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruy_L%C3%B3pez_de_Segura "Ruy López de Segura") and [Gioachino Greco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gioachino_Greco "Gioachino Greco") became widely studied. Chess was the favored game of [Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire "Voltaire"), [Rousseau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rousseau "Rousseau"), [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin") and [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-64)

In 1851, the [first international chess tournament was held in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_1851_chess_tournament "London 1851 chess tournament") and won by [Adolf Anderssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Anderssen "Adolf Anderssen"). Soon after modern [time control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_control "Time control") rules were adopted for competitive play. The first [Official World Chess Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Championship_1886 "World Chess Championship 1886") was held in 1886 in the United States and won by [Wilhelm Steinitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Steinitz "Wilhelm Steinitz"). By the 20th century, the game of [Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") had developed into a [professional sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_sport "Professional sport") with chess clubs, publications, [player ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_rating_system "Chess rating system") and [chess tournaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_tournaments "Chess tournaments"). The [World Chess Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Federation "World Chess Federation") (FIDE) was founded in 1924 in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris").

A large number of [Chess variants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_variants "Chess variants") were also developed, with varying [pieces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairy_chess_pieces "Fairy chess pieces"), rules, boards and scoring. Among them are [Kriegspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kriegspiel_(chess) "Kriegspiel (chess)"), [Capablanca Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capablanca_Chess "Capablanca Chess"), [Alice Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Chess "Alice Chess"), [Circular chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_chess "Circular chess"), [Three-dimensional chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-dimensional_chess "Three-dimensional chess"), [Hexagonal Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagonal_Chess "Hexagonal Chess"), [Chess with different armies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_with_different_armies "Chess with different armies"), and [Bobby Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Fischer "Bobby Fischer")'s [Chess960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess960 "Chess960").

In [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_(game) "Go (game)") and [Shogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shogi "Shogi") became the major board games played at a professional level. Both games were promoted in [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") by the [Tokugawa shogunate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokugawa_shogunate "Tokugawa shogunate") in the 17th century, and top players ([Meijin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meijin "Meijin")) received government endowments. During the 20th century the Japan Shogi Association and the [Japan Go Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Go_Association "Japan Go Association") were founded and began organizing professional tournaments. During the [Qing dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty"), many [Xiangqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiangqi "Xiangqi") clubs were formed and books published. The [Chinese Xiangqi Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Xiangqi_Association "Chinese Xiangqi Association") was formed in 1962, and Xiangqi tournaments are held worldwide by national Xiangqi associations.

In 1997 the first [Mind Sports Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mind_Sports_Olympiad "Mind Sports Olympiad") was held in London and included traditional as well as modern board games. Other board games such as [Backgammon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backgammon "Backgammon"), _[Scrabble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrabble "Scrabble")_ and _[Risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk\_(game) "Risk (game)")_ are also played professionally with dedicated world championships.

### Commercial board games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Commercial board games")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Gyan_Chaupar_National_Museum_India.JPG/250px-Gyan_Chaupar_National_Museum_India.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gyan_Chaupar_National_Museum_India.JPG)

[Gyan chauper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyan_chauper "Gyan chauper"), Late 18th century [Jain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jain "Jain") game board on cloth in the decorative arts gallery of the [National Museum of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_India "National Museum of India"). Acc. No. 85.312

The Ancient Indian game of [Pachisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachisi "Pachisi") was brought to the west by the British in the 1863 and an adaptation of the oldest game named [Parcheesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parcheesi "Parcheesi") was first copyrighted in the United States by EG Selchow & Co in 1869.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-65) A version of the game called _[Ludo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludo\_(board\_game) "Ludo (board game)")_ was patented in 1896. A similar German race game, [Mensch ärgere dich nicht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mensch_%C3%A4rgere_dich_nicht "Mensch ärgere dich nicht") ("Man, don't get annoyed"), became immensely popular with German troops during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). Another Indian game which was adopted by the West was [Gyan chauper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyan_chauper "Gyan chauper") (a.k.a. Moksha Patam), popularly known as [snakes and ladders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snakes_and_ladders "Snakes and ladders"). This was a game which was intended to teach lessons about [karma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karma "Karma") and good and bad actions, the ladders represented virtues and the snakes vices. The moral lesson of the game was that spiritual liberation, or [Moksha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moksha "Moksha") could only be achieved through virtuous action, while vice led to endless reincarnation. The game dates to medieval India where it was played by Jains and Hindus. A Buddhist version, known as "ascending the [spiritual] levels" (Tibetan: _sa gnon rnam bzhags_) is played in Nepal and Tibet[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-66) while a Muslim version of the game played during the [Mughal period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire") from the late 17th or early 18th centuries featured the 101 names of God. The game was first brought to Victorian England and it was published in the United States as _Chutes and Ladders_ (an "improved new version of England's famous indoor sport") by game pioneer [Milton Bradley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Bradley "Milton Bradley") in 1943.

The first board game for which the name of its designer is known is 'A Journey Through Europe or the Play of Geography', a map-based game published in 1759 by [John Jefferys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jefferys "John Jefferys"), a [Geography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography "Geography") and writing teacher.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-67) Designed in England by George Fox in 1800, _[The Mansion of Happiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mansion\_of\_Happiness "The Mansion of Happiness")_ became the prototype for commercial board games for at least two centuries to follow. The first board game published in the United States was _[Traveller's Tour Through the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travellers'\_Tour\_Through\_the\_United\_States "Travellers' Tour Through the United States")_, published by New York City bookseller F. Lockwood in 1822. The earliest board games published in the United States were based upon Christian morality and included _The Mansion of Happiness_ (1843) and _The Game of Pope or Pagan, or The Siege of the Stronghold of Satan by the Christian Army_ (1844). While demonstrating the commercial viability of the ancient race game format, its moralistic overtones were countered by [Milton Bradley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Bradley "Milton Bradley") in 1860 with the introduction of a radically different concept of success in _[The Checkered Game of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Checkered\_Game\_of\_Life "The Checkered Game of Life")_, in which material successes came as a result of accomplishments such as attending college, marrying, and getting rich. Likewise the [Game of the District Messenger Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_the_District_Messenger_Boy "Game of the District Messenger Boy") (1886) also focused on secular capitalist virtues rather than the religious.

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/District_Messenger_Boy_Box_Cover_1886.jpg/250px-District_Messenger_Boy_Box_Cover_1886.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:District_Messenger_Boy_Box_Cover_1886.jpg)

The _Game of the [District Messenger Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph\_boys "Telegraph boys")_ (1886) encouraged the [rags to riches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rags_to_riches "Rags to riches") idea that a lowly messenger boy could ascend the corporate ladder to become president

First patented in 1904, _[The Landlord's Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Landlord's\_Game "The Landlord's Game")_, designed by [Lizzie Magie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lizzie_Magie "Lizzie Magie"),[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-68) was originally intended to illustrate the economic consequences of [Ricardo's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_rent "Law of rent") of [Economic rent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_rent "Economic rent") and the [Georgist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgism "Georgism") concept of a [single tax on land value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_value_tax "Land value tax").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-69) A series of [board games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_game "Board game") were developed from 1906 through the 1930s that involved the buying and selling of land and the development of that land. By 1933, a board game had been created much like the version of modern _[Monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly\_(game) "Monopoly (game)")_ by the [Parker Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parker_Brothers "Parker Brothers").

Though the first commercial version of the [game of _Battleship_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship_(game) "Battleship (game)") was _Salvo_, published in 1931 in the United States by the Starex company, the game itself dates to before [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") when it was played on paper by Russian officers.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-milwaukee-70) The French board game _L'Attaque_ was first commercially released in 1910, having been designed two years prior as a military-themed imperfect knowledge game based upon the earlier Chinese children's board game [dou shou qi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dou_shou_qi "Dou shou qi"). _L'Attaque_ was subsequently adapted by the Chinese into [Luzhanqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzhanqi "Luzhanqi") (or _Lu Zhan Jun Qi_), and by [Milton Bradley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Bradley "Milton Bradley") into [Stratego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratego "Stratego"), the latter having been trademarked in 1960 while the former remains in the public domain. _[Jury Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury\_Box\_(game) "Jury Box (game)")_, published in 1935, was the first [murder mystery game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_mystery_game "Murder mystery game") which served as the basis for games like _[Cluedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluedo "Cluedo")_.

Initially designed in 1938, _[Scrabble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrabble "Scrabble")_ received its first mass-market exposure in 1952, two years prior to the release of _[Diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomacy\_(game) "Diplomacy (game)")_, in 1954. _[Diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomacy\_(game) "Diplomacy (game)")_ was a game favored by [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"), and [Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger"). Originally released in 1957 as _La Conquête du Monde_ ("The Conquest of the World") in France, _[Risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk\_(game) "Risk (game)")_ was first published under its English title in 1959.

Starting with _[Gettysburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg\_(game) "Gettysburg (game)")_ in 1958, the company [Avalon Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon_Hill "Avalon Hill") developed particular board wargames covering specific historical themes such as _[Midway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway\_(1964\_game) "Midway (1964 game)")_, _[D-Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D-Day\_(board\_game) "D-Day (board game)")_ and _[PanzerBlitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PanzerBlitz "PanzerBlitz")_. [Board wargames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_wargame "Board wargame") such as _[Squad Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squad\_Leader "Squad Leader")_, _[Tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactics\_(game) "Tactics (game)")_ and _[Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa\_(wargame) "Europa (wargame)")_ developed extremely complex and realistic rules. Avalon Hill's _[Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization\_(1980\_board\_game) "Civilization (1980 board game)")_ introduced the use of the technology tree (or "tech tree"), variants of which have been implemented in numerous later board and [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_games "Video games") such as _[Sid Meier's Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization\_(video\_game) "Civilization (video game)")_. Recent [wargames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wargaming "Wargaming") such as 'A distant plain', 'Labyrinth' and the satirical _[War on Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War\_on\_Terror\_(game) "War on Terror (game)")_ have focused on counterinsurgency and contemporary [terrorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism "Terrorism").

A concentrated design movement towards the [German-style board game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-style_board_game "German-style board game"), or _Eurogame_, began in the late 1970s and early 1980s in Germany,[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-71) and led to the development of board games such as _[Carcassonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carcassonne\_(board\_game) "Carcassonne (board game)")_, _[The Settlers of Catan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Settlers\_of\_Catan "The Settlers of Catan")_, _[Agricola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricola\_(board\_game) "Agricola (board game)")_, _[Ticket to ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticket\_to\_Ride\_(board\_game) "Ticket to Ride (board game)")_ and _[Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto\_Rico\_(board\_game) "Puerto Rico (board game)")_.

### Card games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Card games")]

Main article: [Card game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_game "Card game")

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/British_soldiers_at_play_France_%28Photo_24-320%29.jpg/250px-British_soldiers_at_play_France_%28Photo_24-320%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:British_soldiers_at_play_France_(Photo_24-320).jpg)

British soldiers playing cards in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), 1915

During the 15th century [card suits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suit_(cards) "Suit (cards)") began to approach the contemporary regional styles and the court cards evolved to represent European royalty. Early European card games included [noddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noddy_(card_game) "Noddy (card game)"), [triomphe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triomphe "Triomphe"), [all fours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_fours_(card_game) "All fours (card game)"), [piquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piquet "Piquet"), [basset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basset_(card_game) "Basset (card game)"), [Hofamterspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hofamterspiel "Hofamterspiel"), [Karnöffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karn%C3%B6ffel "Karnöffel"), and [primero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primero "Primero"). In 1674 [Charles Cotton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Cotton "Charles Cotton") published his _[Compleat Gamester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compleat\_Gamester "Compleat Gamester")_, one of the first books which set out to outline rules for many card and dice games. During the mid-16th century, Portuguese traders introduced playing cards to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"). The first reference to _twenty-one_, the precursor of [blackjack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackjack "Blackjack") is found in a book by the Spanish author [Miguel de Cervantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes "Miguel de Cervantes"). Cervantes was a [gambler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambler "Gambler"), and the main characters of his tale _[Rinconete y Cortadillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rinconete\_y\_Cortadillo "Rinconete y Cortadillo")_ are cheats proficient at playing _ventiuna_ (twenty-one).

The game of [cribbage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cribbage "Cribbage") appears to have developed in the early 17th century, as an adaptation of the earlier card game [noddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noddy_(card_game) "Noddy (card game)"). [Pinochle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinochle "Pinochle") was likely derived from the earlier [bezique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bezique "Bezique"), a game popular in France during the 17th century. 1742 saw the publication of [Edmund Hoyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Hoyle "Edmund Hoyle")'s _Short Treatise on the Game of Whist_ which became one of the bestselling publications of the 18th century.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-72)[Whist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whist "Whist") was widely played during the 18th and 19th centuries,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-73) having evolved from the 16th century game of _trump_ (or _ruff_) by way of [Ruff and Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruff_and_Honours "Ruff and Honours").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-75)

[Baccarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baccarat_(card_game) "Baccarat (card game)") first came to the attention of the public at large and grew to be widely played as a direct result of the [Royal Baccarat Scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Baccarat_Scandal "Royal Baccarat Scandal") of 1891,[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-77) and bears resemblances to the card games [Faro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faro_(card_game) "Faro (card game)") and [Basset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basset_(card_game) "Basset (card game)"), both of which were very popular during the 19th century. The rules of [Contract bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_bridge "Contract bridge") were originally published in 1925, the game having been derived from Bridge games with rules published as early as 1886, Bridge games, in turn, having evolved from the earlier game of Whist.

The first documented game of [poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poker "Poker") dates from an 1833 Mississippi river steamer.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-78) During the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") the game was popular with soldiers and additions were made including [stud poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stud_poker "Stud poker"), and the [straight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_(poker) "Straight (poker)"). Modern [tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poker_tournament "Poker tournament") play became popular in [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") casinos after the [World Series of Poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Series_of_Poker "World Series of Poker") (WSOP) began, in 1970.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-79) Poker's popularity experienced [an unprecedented spike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poker_boom "Poker boom") at the beginning of the 21st century, largely because of the introduction of [online poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_poker "Online poker") and [hole-card cameras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hole-card_camera "Hole-card camera"), which turned the game into a [spectator sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectator_sport "Spectator sport"). In 2009 the [International Federation of Poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_Poker "International Federation of Poker") was founded in [Lausanne, Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lausanne,_Switzerland "Lausanne, Switzerland"), becoming the official governing body for poker.

[Collectible card games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collectible_card_game "Collectible card game") or trading card games while bearing similarities to earlier games in concept, first achieved wide popularity in the 1990s. The first trading card game was _The Base Ball Card Game_ produced by The Allegheny Card Co. and registered on 4 April 1904. It featured 104 unique baseball cards with individual player attributes printed on the cards enabling each collector to build a team and play the game against another person.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-80) The 1990s saw the rise of games such as _[Magic: The Gathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic:\_The\_Gathering "Magic: The Gathering")_ and the _[Pokémon Trading Card Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Trading\_Card\_Game "Pokémon Trading Card Game")_.

### Miniature wargaming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Miniature wargaming")]

Main article: [Miniature wargaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miniature_wargaming "Miniature wargaming")

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/HG_Wells_playing_to_Little_Wars.jpg/250px-HG_Wells_playing_to_Little_Wars.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HG_Wells_playing_to_Little_Wars.jpg)

[H. G. Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._G._Wells "H. G. Wells") playing _[Little Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Wars "Little Wars")_

[Miniature figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miniature_figure_(gaming) "Miniature figure (gaming)") games have their origin in a German chess variant called 'The King's Game', created in 1780 by Helwig, Master of Pages to the Duke of Brunswick. It had a board with 1,666 squares of varying types of terrain, with pieces representing modern military units.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-81) In the early 19th century, the [Prussian army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussian_army "Prussian army") developed war games or 'kriegspieler', with staff officers moving pieces around on a game table, using dice rolls to indicate chance or "friction" and with an umpire scoring the results. After the stunning Prussian [victories against Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Prussian_War "Austro-Prussian War")[and France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War "Franco-Prussian War") in the 19th century, the [Austrians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") and [Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") all began to make use of wargaming as a training tool. By 1889 wargaming was firmly embedded in the culture of the U.S. Navy.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-82)

The first non-military wargame rules were developed by Naval enthusiast and analyst [Fred T. Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_T._Jane "Fred T. Jane") in 1898. [H. G. Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._G._Wells "H. G. Wells") published rules in his _[Floor Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor\_Games "Floor Games")_ (1911) and _[Little Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Wars "Little Wars")_ (1913) designed for wargaming with toy soldiers. In 1956, [Jack Scruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Scruby "Jack Scruby"), known as the "Father of Modern Miniature Wargaming" organized the first miniatures convention and he was also a manufacturer of military miniatures and editor of a wargaming newsletter. Miniature war games became affordable and mainstream in the late 1950s with the rise of cheaper miniature production methods by miniature figure manufacturers such as Scruby Miniatures, Miniature Figurines and Hinchliffe. During the 1980s there was a boom in miniature wargaming with the development of games such as _[Warhammer Fantasy Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warhammer\_Fantasy\_Battle "Warhammer Fantasy Battle")_ and _[Warhammer 40,000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warhammer\_40,000 "Warhammer 40,000")_. Today miniature wargaming includes most historical eras, fantasy and science fiction settings as well as [Naval wargaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_wargaming "Naval wargaming") (_[Don't Give Up the Ship!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't\_Give\_Up\_the\_Ship! "Don't Give Up the Ship!")_, [General Quarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Quarters_(rules) "General Quarters (rules)")), [Air wargaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_wargaming "Air wargaming") and [Space combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_combat "Space combat") wargames (_[Full Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full\_Thrust "Full Thrust")_, _[Attack Vector: Tactical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack\_Vector:\_Tactical "Attack Vector: Tactical")_).

### Role playing games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Role playing games")]

Main article: [History of role-playing games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_role-playing_games "History of role-playing games")

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/D%26D_Game_1.jpg/250px-D%26D_Game_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:D&D_Game_1.jpg)

_[Dungeons & Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeons\_&\_Dragons "Dungeons & Dragons")_ game in progress

Early role-playing games such as those made by [M. A. R. Barker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._A._R._Barker "M. A. R. Barker") and [Greg Stafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Stafford_(game_designer) "Greg Stafford (game designer)") developed from miniature figure wargames. [Gary Gygax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Gygax "Gary Gygax") of the [University of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota "University of Minnesota")'s wargaming society developed a set of rules for a late [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") milieu. This game was called [Chainmail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainmail_(game) "Chainmail (game)") and was a historical game, but later editions included an appendix for adding fantasy elements such as spells, wizards and dragons. By 1971, [Dave Arneson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Arneson "Dave Arneson") had developed a miniatures game called _[Blackmoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackmoor\_(campaign\_setting) "Blackmoor (campaign setting)")_ which contained elements that would become widespread in fantasy gaming: [hit points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_point "Hit point"), [experience points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_point "Experience point"), character levels, [armor class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armor_class "Armor class"), and [dungeon crawls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeon_crawl "Dungeon crawl"). Arneson and Gygax then met and collaborated on the first _[Dungeons & Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeons\_&\_Dragons "Dungeons & Dragons")_ game which was released in 1974 by Gygax's [TSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSR_(company) "TSR (company)"). The game was very successful and several other games such as the Science fiction RPG [Traveller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traveller_(role-playing_game) "Traveller (role-playing game)") and the generic [GURPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GURPS "GURPS") system followed in imitation. In the late 1970s TSR launched _Advanced Dungeons & Dragons_ (AD&D) which saw an expansion of rulebooks and additions. The 1980s saw several [_Dungeons & Dragons_ controversies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeons_&_Dragons_controversies "Dungeons & Dragons controversies") such as the claims that the game promoted [Satanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satanism "Satanism") and [witchcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witchcraft "Witchcraft"). Traditional Roleplaying games were the basis for the modern [Role-playing video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-playing_video_game "Role-playing video game").

### Other indoor games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Other indoor games")]

In [colonial America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_America "Colonial America"), the game of [hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_(game) "Hazard (game)") was called _crapaud_ by the French in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") (a French word meaning "toad" in reference to the original style of play by people crouched over a floor or sidewalk). This was later shortened to [craps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craps "Craps") and after several adaptations became the most popular gambling dice game in the United States.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-83)[Sic bo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic_bo "Sic bo") was introduced into the United States by Chinese immigrants in the 20th century and is now a popular [casino game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino_game "Casino game"). Another casino game, [roulette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roulette "Roulette"), has been played since the late 18th century, and was probably adapted from English wheel games such as Roly-Poly and E.O.

With the possible exception of [carrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrom "Carrom") (a game whose origins are uncertain), the earliest [table games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino_game#Table_games "Casino game") appear to have been the [cue sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_sports "Cue sports"), which include [carom billiards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carom_billiards "Carom billiards"), [pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_(cue_sports) "Pool (cue sports)"), or _pocket billiards_, and [snooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snooker "Snooker"). The cue sports are generally regarded as having developed into indoor games from outdoor stick-and-ball [lawn games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_game "Lawn game") (retroactively termed [ground billiards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_billiards "Ground billiards")),[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-84) and as such to be related to [trucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trucco "Trucco"), [croquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croquet "Croquet") and golf, and more distantly to the stickless [bocce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bocce "Bocce") and [bowls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowls "Bowls").

[Dominoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominoes "Dominoes"), which originate in China and date as far back as the [Song dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_dynasty "Song dynasty") (A.D. 1120), first appeared in Europe during the 18th century. The Chinese [tile game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tile_based_games "Tile based games")[mahjong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahjong "Mahjong") developed from a Chinese card game known as _mǎdiào_ sometime during the 17th century and was imported into the United States in the 1920s.

### Outdoor games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Outdoor games")]

Main article: [History of sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_sport "History of sport")

Modern [sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports "Sports") developed from different European games, many of them played by European royalty. [Tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") developed in France, French kings like [Francis I of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France") (1515–1547) and [Henry II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_II_of_France "Henry II of France") (1547–1559) were well known players. [Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf") originated in Scotland, where the first written record of golf is James II's banning of the game in 1457. The ban was lifted by James IV in 1502 who also played golf. [Cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket") can be traced back to Tudor times in early 16th-century England and the modern rules of [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") and [rugby football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") are based on mid-19th century rules made to standardise the football games played by [English public schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_public_schools "English public schools"). These team sports were spread worldwide by the influence of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire").

### Electronic games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_games&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Electronic games")]

Main articles: [Electronic game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_game "Electronic game") and [History of video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_video_games "History of video games")

The earliest reference to a purely electronic game appears to be a United States patent registration in 1947 for what was described by its inventors as a "[cathode-ray tube amusement device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode-ray_tube_amusement_device "Cathode-ray tube amusement device")".[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-85) Through the 1950s and 1960s the majority of early computer games ran on university [mainframe computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Beginning in 1971, video [arcade games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_game "Arcade game") began to be offered to the public for play. The first [home video game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console "Video game console"), the [Magnavox Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnavox_Odyssey "Magnavox Odyssey"), was released in 1972.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gaming#cite_note-87)

The [golden age of arcade video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_age_of_arcade_video_games "Golden age of arcade video games") began in 1978 and continued through to the mid-1980s. A [second generation of video game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Second generation of video game consoles"), released between 1977 and 1983, saw increased popularity as a result of this, though this eventually came to an abrupt end with the [video game crash of 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_crash_of_1983 "Video game crash of 1983"). The home [video game industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_industry "Video game industry") was eventually revitalized with the [third generation of game consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Third generation of video game consoles") over the next few years, which saw a shift in the dominance of the video game industry from the United States to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"). This same time period saw the advent of the [personal computer game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer_game "Personal computer game"), specialized gaming [home computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_computer "Home computer"), early [online gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_game "Online game"), and the introduction of [LED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED "LED")[handheld electronic games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_electronic_game "Handheld electronic game") and eventually [handheld video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_video_game "Handheld video game").
